The surest sign that you should walk away from an SEO proposal is a guarantee of first-page or number-one rankings. Google's own guidance for people hiring an SEO says that no one can guarantee a top ranking in Google, and that anyone claiming a special relationship with Google or secret access to its systems is not telling the truth. That single red flag removes a large share of the proposals a business owner in Pune will receive. But it is only the first of several, and some of the most expensive problems come from agencies that avoid the obvious promises and still do harmful or empty work. If you are weighing a digital marketing agency in Pune for SEO, this guide gives you the warning signs, the questions to ask, what honest work looks like, what to put in a contract, and how to check what you are paying for. It is written for the business owner, school administrator, clinic manager or NGO trustee who is not an SEO but is about to sign one.

We rely on Google Search Central's published guidance, mainly "Do you need an SEO?", the Google Search spam policies and the documentation for Search Console's manual actions report. Where we describe our own practice as a company that does this work, we say so. We quote no prices for Pune SEO retainers because we have no independent source for a market range, and an invented one would mislead you. Ask three agencies for written quotes and compare the scope, not only the amount.

## Start with what SEO can and cannot promise

Search engine optimisation is the practice of making a website easier for search engines to understand and more useful to people, so that it can appear for relevant searches. Google's documentation says plainly that SEO changes are generally gradual and that results take time. Google also says that it makes no guarantees about when or whether a page will be crawled, indexed or ranked. An agency can promise work, and it can promise reports, but it cannot promise a position, because the position is decided by Google's systems, by your competitors, and by searchers' behaviour, none of which the agency controls.

This leads to a useful test for any proposal. Promises about activities are fine: "we will fix these 40 technical issues, write six pages and report monthly". Promises about outcomes controlled by someone else are not: "page one in 30 days". The first can be checked. The second cannot, and when it fails the agency will have a ready explanation.

## The red flags, from most to least serious

### 1. A guaranteed ranking

"First page guaranteed" or "number one for your keywords in 60 days". Google's guidance on hiring an SEO addresses this directly. Be wary even of softer versions, such as "money-back if you do not rank" with conditions in the small print that make a refund impossible. The conditions usually specify obscure keywords nobody searches for, which are easy to rank for and bring no customers.

### 2. Secret methods and a special relationship

"We have inside contacts at Google", "our proprietary system", "we cannot tell you how it works". Google's guidance says that no one can claim a special relationship that gives preferential ranking. A competent SEO can explain what they will change and why, in plain language. If they cannot or will not, you are paying for something you cannot evaluate.

### 3. Buying or building links to manipulate ranking

Google's spam policies list link spam, which includes buying or selling links that pass ranking credit, excessive link exchanges, and large-scale automated link creation. A proposal that includes "50 high-authority backlinks per month" without saying where they come from probably involves paying for placements on sites that sell them. Google's systems are built to neutralise such links, and a pattern of them can contribute to a manual action. Genuine links come from being cited by relevant sites, local organisations, suppliers, associations, press and partners. That is slow, and cannot be priced as a fixed monthly quantity.

### 4. Mass-produced content

Google's spam policies include scaled content abuse: generating large volumes of pages primarily to manipulate rankings, whether by automation, humans or a mix, without adding value for readers. An agency offering "100 blog posts in a month" or "a page for every locality in Maharashtra" is describing a risk, not a service. We have written about the local version of this, in our guide to [service-area pages that do not become doorway pages](/blog/website-designer-pune-service-area-location-pages-doorway-2026/). A small number of pages that answer real questions is the better investment.

### 5. Hidden text, cloaking and doorway pages

Text coloured to match the background, keywords placed off-screen, different content shown to Google than to visitors, and near-duplicate pages that funnel to one destination are all listed in Google's spam policies. If an agency adds text to your pages that visitors cannot see, you carry the penalty, not the agency. Ask them directly: "will any text on my site be invisible to visitors?" The only acceptable answer is no.

### 6. Taking over your accounts and domains in their own name

If the agency registers your domain, hosting, Google Business Profile, Search Console or Analytics under its own account, you have lost control, and moving away later becomes a negotiation. Everything about your business should be registered in your name, with the agency added as a user. See our [website handover and ownership checklist](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-handover-ownership-checklist-2026/) for what to demand.

### 7. Unsolicited outreach with a "free audit"

Google's guidance warns about unsolicited emails and messages promising rankings. An automated "audit" that lists hundreds of scary issues, many of them trivial, and ends with "we can fix this for a monthly fee" is a sales tool. Treat a cold audit as marketing. A useful audit is specific to your site, is explained by a person, and prioritises the few things that matter.

### 8. Vague deliverables

"SEO optimisation: monthly" with no list of tasks. If you cannot tell what you are buying, you cannot tell whether it was delivered. Our guide to [what a retainer should list and report](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-retainer-deliverables-reporting-2026/) shows the shape of a clear scope.

### 9. Reports full of vanity numbers

Impressions, "keywords ranking", "domain authority" and traffic are easy to inflate and do not pay salaries. A report that celebrates a rise in keyword count while enquiries are flat is decoration. See our piece on [which numbers in a monthly marketing report matter](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-monthly-marketing-report-metrics-that-matter-2026/).

### 10. No questions about your business

An agency that quotes before learning what you sell, who buys it, where your customers are and what an enquiry is worth is selling a package. Good SEO starts with your commercial reality: which searches would bring someone who might actually buy.

## What honest SEO work looks like

Honest SEO is mostly unglamorous. In our own practice, and consistent with Google's SEO starter guidance, the work falls into five areas.

**Technical foundations.** Making sure the site can be crawled and indexed, loads reasonably fast, works on mobile, uses HTTPS, has a sensible URL structure and sitemap, and does not accidentally block itself. Our guide on [why a new website may not be on Google](/blog/web-development-company-pune-new-website-not-on-google-crawled-not-indexed-2026/) shows how common the accidental problems are.

**Search intent and page planning.** Deciding which searches to target and which page answers each one, with one clear purpose per page. See [keyword research and search intent mapping](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-keyword-research-search-intent-mapping-2026/).

**Content that answers real questions.** Pages written by someone who knows the subject, with specifics such as prices, timelines and what is included, rather than generic text.

**Local presence, where relevant.** A verified and well-maintained Google Business Profile, consistent business details and honest reviews, as covered in our [Google reviews guide](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-business-profile-reviews-2026/) and our [local SEO overview](/blog/local-seo-google-map-pack-pune-2026/).

**Earning mentions and links legitimately.** Being listed by relevant associations, publishing something worth citing, and being useful to local press and partners.

None of that can be bought in a week, which is why guarantees are suspicious.

## Questions to ask before you sign

Put these to every agency. The quality of the answer matters more than the answer.

1. **What exactly will you do in the first 90 days, in a list?** Look for specific tasks, not categories.
2. **Which pages will you change or create, and who writes them?** Ask to see writing samples.
3. **Will any text or links on my site be invisible to visitors?** The answer must be no.
4. **Where will links come from?** If the answer involves buying them or a network of sites they own, decline.
5. **Whose name will my accounts be in?** It must be yours.
6. **Will I have access to Search Console and Analytics?** Yes, as owner.
7. **How will you measure success, and what is the baseline?** Look for enquiries, calls and qualified leads, not only rankings.
8. **What will you not do?** An honest agency has limits. One that does everything is selling.
9. **Can I speak to a client with a similar business?** Ask for permission-based references, and be wary of case studies without names or verifiable details.
10. **What happens if I leave?** You should keep your content, accounts and data, with a clean handover.
11. **How do you use AI to produce content, and who reviews it?** AI-assisted writing is not banned, but Google's spam policies target mass-produced content that adds no value. The agency should name the human who checks facts.
12. **What risks come with your approach?** A confident answer that mentions none is a warning.

## How to check an agency's claims

Some claims can be verified independently in an afternoon.

- **Search for the agency's own ranking.** An agency that sells SEO should be findable for something related to its own business. This proves little on its own, but a complete absence is worth noticing. Remember that the SERP for generic phrases may be dominated by listicles, and do not judge on one phrase.
- **Check their case studies.** Are the clients named? Is the website live? Does the claimed result match what you can see, for example the client's site actually appearing for the searches described? Where numbers are given, ask how they were measured. We caution against taking unnamed percentages at face value.
- **Search the agency name with "reviews" and "complaints".** Read both good and bad, and judge the pattern.
- **Look at the work on their own website.** Is it written by a person with expertise, with specifics, or filled with generic text and keyword repetition?
- **Ask about the process in your first call.** Notice whether they ask about your business or open with their package.

## What to put in the contract

A contract does not make the agency competent, but it protects you from the common failures. We suggest asking for:

- **A scope list** of monthly activities, with the number of pages, fixes and reports, and the length of the commitment.
- **Ownership clause:** all domains, hosting, Search Console, Analytics, Business Profile and content belong to you from day one.
- **Access:** you are an owner on every account, and the agency is an added user.
- **A prohibition on spam techniques:** no hidden text, no purchased links, no automated mass content, no fake reviews, and no cloaking, with the agency accepting responsibility for damage caused by breach. Be realistic about enforceability, but make the expectation clear.
- **Reporting:** a monthly report in plain language, with the metrics agreed in advance, and a call to discuss it.
- **A notice period** you can live with, rather than a long lock-in.
- **Handover on exit:** documents, credentials and a list of everything changed.
- **Change log:** a record of every significant change to your site.

Avoid contracts that tie you to a long term in exchange for a discount with no exit if the work is poor.

## If you already have a problem

If you suspect a past agency did harm, check these:

1. **Search Console, Manual actions report.** If Google has applied a manual action, it appears there with a reason. Google's documentation describes the steps to fix the issue and submit a reconsideration request. Not every ranking drop is a manual action; most are not.
2. **Search Console, Security issues report.** Hacked content can mimic SEO decay.
3. **Your link profile.** Look at the links Search Console reports. Google's documentation says disavowing is an advanced tool, mostly unnecessary, and that the problem usually lies with links you paid for or made yourself. Seek advice before using it.
4. **Your pages.** Look for hidden text, strange pages you did not approve, and mass-produced content.
5. **Your accounts.** Confirm you are the owner of the domain, hosting and Google properties.
6. **Timing.** Compare the date of any drop against changes made, and against known Google updates, before blaming anyone. Drops have many causes, including simple technical errors, as we explain in our guide to [content refresh and decay audits](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-seo-content-refresh-decay-audit-2026/).

If you want a second opinion on an existing agency's work, a short independent review of your accounts and site is a reasonable expense, and we do such reviews as well.

## A fair expectation of timing

Google's guidance says that SEO work generally takes time to show effects and gives no guarantees. A realistic plan treats the first months as foundation work, fixing technical problems and publishing the right pages, followed by gradual improvement that depends on your competition. We would not trust anyone, including ourselves, who gives you a precise number of weeks. Judge the first quarter by completed work and by early signals such as pages being indexed and impressions appearing in Search Console, and judge the following quarters by enquiries.

Sometimes the honest advice is that SEO is not the right first spend. A business with a slow, broken or unclear website often gets more from fixing the site first. A business that needs enquiries this month may be better served by well-run [Google Ads](/services/google-ads/) while the organic work builds. And a business with no local profile may be better served by setting that up properly first. An agency that recommends only what it sells is not advising you.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can an SEO company guarantee first-page rankings on Google?

No. Google's guidance for hiring an SEO says that no one can guarantee a top ranking and that claims of a special relationship with Google are not true. An agency can commit to specific work and reporting, but it cannot control where Google places a page.

### How do I know if an SEO agency is using spam techniques?

Ask whether any text or links will be invisible to visitors, where links will come from, and how content will be produced. Google's spam policies list hidden text, link spam, cloaking, doorway pages and scaled content abuse. Check Search Console's Manual actions report for any action already applied.

### How long does SEO take to work?

Google says results take time and gives no guarantee, so be wary of anyone quoting a precise number of weeks. Judge early months by completed technical and content work and by signals such as indexing and impressions, and later months by enquiries.

### Should I give an SEO agency ownership of my website or Google accounts?

No. Register your domain, hosting, Search Console, Analytics and Business Profile in your own name, and add the agency as a user. Ownership in the agency's account makes leaving difficult.

### What should an SEO proposal include?

A list of specific monthly tasks, who writes content, how success is measured against a baseline, what the agency will not do, the length and exit terms of the contract, and a prohibition on spam techniques. Vague promises of optimisation are a warning.
